screens.title: Chaincode Development Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Secure, maintainable, and performant smart contracts for Hyperledger Fabric

narration.text: In this lesson we will set the stage for writing chaincode that stays secure and maintainable over time. You will learn why input validation and access control are the first lines of defense, how to model ledger state so queries remain efficient, and how to plan for upgrades and testing so that fixes and new features can be deployed without jeopardizing the network. I will illustrate practical techniques such as using the Client Identity Chaincode Library for identity checks, creating composite keys for efficient queries, and building unit tests with the mock shim to catch issues early. We will also cover pitfalls to avoid, like non-deterministic operations and storing large binaries on the ledger. By the end you should be able to design chaincode functions that validate inputs, enforce roles, scale their state model, and include tests and migration paths. Think of this chapter as a checklist you can apply whenever you write or review chaincode: validate, authorize, model, test, and plan for upgrades. To begin, notice the key topics listed below: access control, state design, upgradeability and testing — each will become a concrete practice you can apply in your next deployment.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Treat chaincode like critical infrastructure: validate inputs, enforce identity-based permissions, design lean state, and include tests and upgrades in every release.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.2 › Chaincode Development Best Practices

Chaincode Development Best Practices

Build chaincode that is secure, efficient, and upgradeable. This lesson focuses on practical steps you can take today.

In this lesson
Validate, authorize, model state, test, and prepare upgrades.
Why it matters
Chaincode mistakes are hard to fix after deployment; good practices prevent vulnerabilities and performance problems.
Audience
Developers, reviewers, and validators responsible for chaincode design and deployment.
Outcome
Chaincode that validates inputs, enforces roles, scales, and can be upgraded with migrations and tests.
Explore Key Topics
Access Control
Use CID to check MSP IDs and attributes before sensitive operations.
State Design
Composite keys, lean JSON, and off-chain storage for large binaries.
Testing & Upgrades
Unit and integration tests plus migration functions for safe upgrades.
Interactive concept
Secure by default
Fail early on identity or validation errors to minimize wasted compute.
Plan for migration
Include a migration path in upgrades to avoid breaking stored data.
Test locally
Use mock stubs for fast unit tests before integration runs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on practical competencies you will exercise when developing chaincode. First, you will validate and sanitize all inputs and enforce identity-based permissions so that only authorized organizations can run sensitive functions. For example, you will use Fabric's Client Identity APIs to read an MSP ID and compare it to an expected value before creating an asset. Second, you will design efficient state and keys — using composite keys and lean JSON — so queries remain performant and storage on the ledger is minimized. Third, you will design chaincode with upgradeability in mind: increment versions, include migration helpers, and avoid breaking schema changes whenever possible. Finally, you will write both unit tests using the mock shim and integration tests against a temporary network to catch errors that only appear in distributed contexts. Each objective pairs a developer action with why it matters in production, and by achieving them you reduce security risk and operational friction when updating smart contract logic.

keyIdea.title: Objectives summary
keyIdea.text: Master input validation, access control, state modeling, testing, and upgrade planning to produce reliable chaincode.

screens.title: Skills you'll practice
screens.subtitle: Concrete developer actions and verification steps

narration.text: This second objectives screen drills into the developer actions you will practice. You will implement checks that read the submitter's MSP ID and attributes and fail early when the identity is not authorized, reducing wasted endorsement work. You will craft composite keys to support queries across attributes, and maintain slim JSON structures so CouchDB indexes operate efficiently. You will add a versioning plan to your chaincode and write migration functions that transform older records in a controlled invocation, which avoids breaking existing peers during upgrades. Testing will cover both unit-level function behavior using a mocked stub and integration tests run against a temporary network to validate endorsement and ordering interactions. Finally, you will recognize and mitigate non-deterministic operations such as on-chain randomness or uncontrolled timestamps. Practicing these skills in code and tests gives you confidence that your chaincode behaves deterministically and is safe to deploy across organizations.

  • • Use composite keys for multi-attribute queries and design indexes for CouchDB when you need rich JSON search.
  • • Keep ledger payloads lean; store hashes for large off-chain objects to protect performance and privacy.

screens.title: Input Validation: Rules and Patterns
screens.subtitle: Never trust client data — validate types, formats, ranges, and presence

narration.text: Input validation in chaincode is a disciplined process of checking every value that comes from an external client before you use it to update the ledger. Define explicit rules for each parameter: whether it must be non-empty, whether it must parse to an integer or boolean, expected length, and allowed ranges. For example, if a function accepts a size or price, ensure that it parses as an integer and falls within an acceptable lower and upper bound. Always fail fast: return a clear error on the first validation failure so the caller knows why the transaction was rejected. A concrete example from the chapter is verifying an asset creation request by ensuring id, color, and owner are not empty and size is greater than zero. A common misconception is that endorsement policies or client-side checks are sufficient; they are not. Client checks can be bypassed and endorsement ensures ordering, not business logic correctness. Validation belongs inside chaincode because peers execute and endorse the logic. Practical tips: centralize validation helpers to avoid duplication, give descriptive error messages, and validate before performing expensive state lookups to reduce wasted computation. As a takeaway, treat validation as the first layer of defence: it prevents incorrect state, reduces error surfaces during endorsement, and documents business rules for future maintainers. How will you structure reusable validation helpers in your next contract?

keyIdea.title: Validation rule
keyIdea.text: Fail early and explicitly: validate presence, type, format, and range before any state access or mutation.

content.html:
Definition
Input validation

Systematic verification of every external parameter to ensure type safety, length, format and domain rules. Validation prevents bad state and runtime errors during endorsement.

Common patterns
  • Check presence (non-empty) for identifiers and owner fields.
  • Parse and validate numeric ranges for sizes or values.
  • Trim and normalize strings to avoid accidental duplicates.
  • Validate length and permitted characters for IDs.
Key Takeaway

Validation lives in chaincode: it documents rules, prevents bad endorsements, and reduces wasted execution.

Concrete example
// Input validation example (Go)
func validateCreateInput(id string, color string, size int, owner string) error {
  if id == "" || color == "" || owner == "" || size <= 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("asset ID, color, owner, and size must be provided and valid")
  }
  return nil
}
Misconception check

Do not rely on client-side validation or assume only trusted callers will submit correct data. Peers must validate because all transactions get executed and endorsed by peers.

Try this
Create reusable validation helpers, call them at entry points, and add unit tests that pass invalid inputs to confirm errors are returned.

screens.title: Access Control & the Client Identity Library
screens.subtitle: Use MSP ID and attributes to enforce who can call sensitive functions

narration.text: Access control in Fabric chaincode means explicitly checking the identity of the transaction submitter before performing privileged actions. The Client Identity Chaincode Library (CID) and the transaction context provide functions to get the client's MSP ID and attributes. A recommended pattern is to read the MSP ID at the beginning of the function and compare it to allowed MSP IDs, failing early if the caller is unauthorized. For more granular permissions, check certificate attributes that represent roles. The chapter shows an example where only Org1MSP is allowed to create assets. A common mistake is to trust that only certain applications will call an endpoint; network peers cannot assume clients are honest. Another trap is performing expensive validations before authorization; instead, verify identity first to avoid wasted work. Practical example: call ctx. GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID() and compare strings, or use CID helper wrappers to check attributes. When testing, mock the client identity to simulate both authorized and unauthorized callers to ensure the chaincode rejects unauthorized attempts. As a takeaway, make access checks explicit, centralize them if possible, and always fail early to conserve resources and simplify debugging. How will you express role checks in your next contract?

keyIdea.title: Access control rule
keyIdea.text: Always check client identity and attributes at function start and reject unauthorized requests before performing validations or state mutations.

content.html:
Why this matters

Peers execute chaincode for any submitted transaction. Access control inside chaincode ensures only authorized identities can change critical state, preventing unauthorized asset creation or administrative actions.

Patterns
  • Read MSP ID immediately via ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID().
  • Check attributes with CID for role-based permissions.
  • Fail early: return authorization errors before heavy work or state changes.
Pro tip
Centralize authorization checks to a helper function so you reuse consistent logic and messages across handlers.
Code example
// Access control snippet (Go)
clientMSPID, err := ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID()
if err != nil {
  return fmt.Errorf("failed to get client MSP ID: %v", err)
}
if clientMSPID != "Org1MSP" {
  return fmt.Errorf("client not authorized to create assets: %s", clientMSPID)
}
Testing note

When unit testing, mock the creator identity in the stub to simulate authorized and unauthorized MSP IDs and confirm expected responses.

screens.title: Secure CreateAsset Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Integrate access control and input validation in a Go CreateAsset implementation

narration.text: Let's walk through a secure CreateAsset implementation that combines access control and input validation. The function first retrieves the caller's MSP ID and fails if it is not the expected organization. This is an efficient early exit. Next it validates the provided parameters — checking for empty strings and ensuring numeric fields are positive. Only after these checks does it query the ledger to see if the asset already exists. If it does not, the asset is marshaled to JSON and written to state. This order — authorize, validate, then state access — reduces wasted computation and makes log messages clearer. The example in the chapter shows this pattern and returns clear error messages when any step fails. When writing your own code, keep helper functions for authorization checks and validation so your main handler remains readable. Also, avoid leaking internal details in errors; give enough information to debug while preserving security. As a learner, try to modify the example to add attribute-based checks and unit tests that set different MSP IDs to ensure rejection paths work as intended. What additional attributes might you check for administrative functions in your organization?

keyIdea.title: Order of operations
keyIdea.text: Authorize first, validate inputs second, then perform state reads and writes to minimize wasted work and clearer failure modes.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
// Secure CreateAsset (Go)
func (s *SmartContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, id string, color string, size int, owner string) error {
  clientMSPID, err := ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID()
  if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to get client MSP ID: %v", err)
  }
  if clientMSPID != "Org1MSP" {
    return fmt.Errorf("client not authorized to create assets: %s", clientMSPID)
  }

  if id == "" || color == "" || owner == "" || size <= 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("asset ID, color, owner, and size must be provided and valid")
  }

  exists, err := s.AssetExists(ctx, id)
  if err != nil {
    return err
  }
  if exists {
    return fmt.Errorf("the asset %s already exists", id)
  }

  asset := Asset{ID: id, Color: color, Size: size, Owner: owner, AppraisedValue: 0}
  assetJSON, err := json.Marshal(asset)
  if err != nil { return err }

  return ctx.GetStub().PutState(id, assetJSON)
}
Explanation
  • Authorize: Fail if MSP ID is not permitted to reduce wasted operations.
  • Validate: Ensure required fields and ranges before state calls.
  • Existence check: Read to prevent duplicates and return explicit error.
  • Write: Marshal and write only when all checks succeed.
Misconception
Checking existence before authorization may leak information. Decide whether revealing existence is acceptable and prefer authorization first.

screens.title: Designing Ledger State and Keys
screens.subtitle: Composite keys, lean models, and off-chain references

narration.text: State management in Fabric is about designing a key-value layout that supports queries and scales. The ledger is a key-value store, so your choice of keys and JSON structure determines how easy it is to look up records. Composite keys allow queries by multiple attributes without duplicating data. For example, a composite key combining asset type and owner supports listing assets for a given owner efficiently. When you need full-text or attribute-based search, CouchDB enables richer JSON queries, but it requires thoughtfully designed indexes to avoid expensive scans. A crucial rule is to keep on-ledger objects lean: store essential fields, and keep large binaries off-chain by storing a hash or reference to secure object storage. Also, update patterns should follow read-modify-write: always read the current state, modify the object in memory, then write it back. This minimizes race conditions and leverages Fabric's endorsement and MVCC checks. A common misconception is to model everything as nested heavy objects; that makes queries slow and increases endorsement payload sizes. Instead, normalize where useful, use composite keys for querying, and design indexes for CouchDB when rich queries are required. As a takeaway, model for the queries you need and keep the ledger focused on integrity-critical data.

keyIdea.title: State design principle
keyIdea.text: Model state for the queries you need: use composite keys for multi-attribute lookups and keep ledger data lean; reference large objects off-chain.

content.html:
Architecture
Key and data modeling

Choose keys to support access patterns. Composite keys let you query by multiple attributes while keeping each object single-sourced.

Composite key example
CreateCompositeKey("asset~owner~type", []string{assetID, owner, assetType}) lets you perform range queries for a given owner or type by building a prefix.
Why lean matters
Smaller JSON reduces endorsement payloads, speeds replication, and keeps CouchDB index sizes manageable.
Patterns & cautions
  • Store hashes or URIs for large binaries and keep the actual files in secure off-chain storage.
  • Design CouchDB indexes for frequent Mango queries to avoid full scans.
  • Avoid deep nesting of objects that make partial updates complex.
Key takeaway
Design your keys and JSON to match query and update patterns; plan indexes when using CouchDB for rich queries.

screens.title: LevelDB vs CouchDB for State Queries
screens.subtitle: When to use simple key lookups and when to use rich JSON queries

narration.text: Fabric supports both LevelDB and CouchDB as state databases, and choosing between them depends on your query needs. LevelDB is a high-performance embedded key-value store optimized for exact key lookups and range queries. If your access pattern is primarily GetState and GetStateByRange over well-structured keys or composite keys, LevelDB is efficient and predictable. CouchDB enables rich JSON queries using Mango and supports indexing on document fields. Use CouchDB when you need to query by non-key attributes or run complex attribute filters. However, CouchDB queries can become resource-intensive without proper indexes, and large result sets can degrade peer performance. The chapter highlights that CouchDB queries should be indexed and used judiciously. A common misconception is that CouchDB solves all search problems; it does add flexibility but requires additional maintenance and index planning. If you choose CouchDB, design compact documents, add appropriate indexes for frequent queries, and paginate results to avoid timeouts. As a practical rule: model primary access via keys when possible, and enable CouchDB only when attribute-based search is essential. LevelDB vs CouchDB for State Queries means prefer key-based designs with leveldb for most workloads; use couchdb for necessary attribute queries but design indexes and paginate results to control cost.. In practical terms, when to use simple key lookups and when to use rich json queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Selection rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer key-based designs with LevelDB for most workloads; use CouchDB for necessary attribute queries but design indexes and paginate results to control cost.

content.html:
LevelDB
Optimized for exact key lookups and range scans. Use when queries can be satisfied by well-structured keys or composite keys. Fast and low-overhead for most common patterns.
When to use
  • Direct GetState and PutState use cases.
  • Range queries where composite keys provide the index.
CouchDB
Supports rich JSON queries via Mango and index definitions. Useful for attribute-based searches, but requires index planning and can be resource-intensive for large datasets.
Guidance
  • Create indexes for frequent queries to avoid full scans.
  • Paginate and limit results to reduce timeouts and memory use.
Performance tip
Favor key designs for predictable performance and use CouchDB selectively.
Common mistake
Running complex Mango queries without indexes can cause timeouts and heavy CPU use on peers.
Action
If you need CouchDB, define indexes early and test query performance against realistic datasets.

screens.title: Read-Modify-Write and Concurrency
screens.subtitle: Using optimistic concurrency with GetState and PutState

narration.text: Updating state in Fabric follows a read-modify-write pattern and relies on optimistic concurrency control. The typical process is: read the current state with GetState, modify the in-memory object, and then write it back with PutState. Fabric peers check versioning information during endorsement and ordering; if another transaction modified the same key between endorsement and commit, the committing peer will detect a version mismatch and reject the committing transaction. This ensures strong consistency without explicit locks, but it also means you must design for conflict handling. For high-contention keys, consider sharding or splitting state so concurrent writes go to different keys. Avoid long-running logic between read and write because it increases the window for conflicts. A common misconception is to perform many state reads across large datasets inside a single transaction; this increases the chance of conflicts and slows endorsement. Instead, keep transactions focused, perform necessary validations, and design your data model to minimize write hotspots. As a takeaway, rely on Fabric's optimistic concurrency, but structure your chaincode to reduce contention and handle rejected commits gracefully at the client level. Read-Modify-Write and Concurrency means use read-modify-write and design to avoid hotspots; rely on fabric's optimistic concurrency and handle conflicts at the client side.. In practical terms, using optimistic concurrency with getstate and putstate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concurrency rule
keyIdea.text: Use read-modify-write and design to avoid hotspots; rely on Fabric's optimistic concurrency and handle conflicts at the client side.

content.html:
Steps
  1. GetState - Read the current value and version for the key.
  2. Modify - Apply business logic to the in-memory representation.
  3. PutState - Write the updated value back to the ledger; peer MVCC checks detect conflicts.
Design tips
  • Minimize the time between read and write to shrink conflict windows.
  • Split frequently-updated counters or aggregates across multiple keys to avoid hotspots.
  • Handle commit rejections in client code by retrying or surfacing a clear error.
Example scenario

If many clients update the same asset owner field simultaneously, endorsements may conflict. Shard ownership records or queue updates via application logic to reduce collisions.

Misconception
Fabric does not provide locks for application state; optimistic concurrency and MVCC are the intended mechanisms.

screens.title: Upgradeability and Versioning
screens.subtitle: Plan schema changes and include migration helpers

narration.text: Chaincode evolves, and Fabric’s lifecycle lets you deploy new versions without taking the network offline, but careful planning is required to avoid breaking existing data. Always increment your chaincode version when logic changes, and coordinate endorsements across organizations so all peers agree on the new chaincode definition. Avoid breaking schema changes to stored JSON; when you must change structure, implement a migration function that can be invoked during or after upgrade to transform stored records to the new format. Migration functions should be idempotent and able to handle partial runs so you can resume if interrupted. Keep backward-compatible code paths when possible so older data remains readable by the new logic. A common developer mistake is deploying a new chaincode that expects a different JSON layout without migrating the ledger, causing runtime errors during read or unmarshal operations. Include migration unit tests and test upgrades on a temporary network before production. As a practical step, maintain a version field in stored objects when you expect schema evolution; that helps your migration code detect and transform older records safely. The core takeaway is to treat upgrades as planned maintenance with clear migration steps and tests.

keyIdea.title: Upgrade rule
keyIdea.text: Bump versions, coordinate endorsements, and include idempotent migration helpers to preserve data integrity during upgrades.

content.html:
Versioning
Increment chaincode version numbers with each deployment and ensure all organizations approve the new definition before commit.
Migration guidance
  • Include an explicit migration function that transforms old records to the new schema.
  • Make migrations idempotent so they can be safely re-run.
  • Test the upgrade path on a temporary network before production deployment.
Practical tip
Maintain a version field inside persisted objects. Use it to detect old formats and only run migration logic when necessary.
Common pitfall
Deploying incompatible schema without migration causes unmarshal errors and can break transaction handlers on upgraded peers.

screens.title: Unit Testing Chaincode with Mock Stub
screens.subtitle: Mock the ChaincodeStubInterface and test authorization and validation locally

narration.text: Unit testing catches logic bugs before you deploy. Fabric provides a shim that can be mocked so you write fast unit tests without a running network. Use the mock stub to simulate invocations and set a mocked creator identity so you can exercise authorization paths. The chapter provides a simple unit test structure: create a SmartContract instance, create a mock stub, set the creator to an authorized or unauthorized MSP ID, then invoke the function and assert the expected status or error message. Tests should cover success paths, invalid inputs, authorization failures, and error conditions like duplicate creation attempts. A misconception is to skip unit tests because integration tests will catch issues; in reality, unit tests are faster, isolate logic, and help document intent. When designing tests, mock only external dependencies and keep assertions focused on a single behavior. Also add tests for migration helpers and schema transformations. As a practical exercise, write tests that simulate an unauthorized Org2MSP trying to create an asset and confirm the mock invocation returns an error referencing authorization. Unit tests are a fast feedback loop that helps keep chaincode robust as you iterate.

keyIdea.title: Testing rule
keyIdea.text: Use the mock stub to unit test authorization and validation paths quickly; keep tests focused and cover both success and expected failure cases.

content.html:
Unit test example
func TestCreateAsset_Authorized(t *testing.T) {
  scc := new(SmartContract)
  mockStub := shim.NewMockStub("mycc", scc)
  mockStub.SetCreator(getTestCreator("Org1MSP"))

  response := mockStub.MockInvoke("1", [][]byte{
    []byte("CreateAsset"), []byte("asset1"), []byte("blue"), []byte("10"), []byte("Alice"),
  })
  assert.Equal(t, int32(peer.Response_OK), response.Status)
}

func TestCreateAsset_Unauthorized(t *testing.T) {
  scc := new(SmartContract)
  mockStub := shim.NewMockStub("mycc", scc)
  mockStub.SetCreator(getTestCreator("Org2MSP"))

  response := mockStub.MockInvoke("1", [][]byte{
    []byte("CreateAsset"), []byte("asset2"), []byte("red"), []byte("20"), []byte("Bob"),
  })
  assert.Equal(t, int32(peer.Response_ERROR), response.Status)
  assert.Contains(t, response.Message, "client not authorized")
}
Test structure
  • Arrange: instantiate contract and mock stub.
  • Act: set creator and invoke the function.
  • Assert: check status and messages for expected outcomes.
Developer tip
Keep helper functions for creating mock creators so tests are readable and focused on behavior.

screens.title: Integration Testing and Deployment Checks
screens.subtitle: Test upgrades and real endorsement flows on a temporary network

narration.text: Integration testing validates behavior across peers, orderer, and endorsement policies. Use a temporary Fabric network — for example, a test network that deploys peers for the organizations you support — and install the chaincode package, approve definitions, and commit the new chaincode version. Run realistic transactions from SDK clients or the peer CLI to confirm endorsements, transient data behavior, and PutState/GetState interactions across peers. Test both normal and failure paths: unauthorized submissions, invalid inputs, and competing transactions that may trigger MVCC conflicts. Also test upgrades end-to-end: deploy a new chaincode version, run the migration functions, and verify that existing records are readable and behave correctly under the new logic. A common oversight is to only run unit tests and miss integration issues such as endorsement policy mismatches or environment-specific configuration. Integration tests are slower but catch these issues before production. As a practical exercise from the chapter, script packaging, installation, approval, and invocation steps and run both successful and intentionally failing invocations to confirm error handling and logs are informative. The final reflection: can your upgrade be rolled back or retried safely if an error occurs during migration?

keyIdea.title: Integration rule
keyIdea.text: Validate the full deployment and endorsement flow on a temporary network, including upgrade and migration steps, before production rollout.

content.html:
Integration checklist
  • Package and install chaincode on peers for all required orgs.
  • Approve and commit the chaincode definition with correct endorsements.
  • Invoke transactions via SDK or peer CLI to validate endorsements and state changes.
  • Run migration functions and verify transformed records.
Terminal demo style
Script packaging, install, and approval steps, then run both valid and invalid commands to observe success and error responses. Capture logs from peers to diagnose endorsement or schema issues.
Tip
Automate your integration tests in CI so upgrades and migration scripts run before merging changes to mainline branches.

screens.title: Determinism, Performance, and Common Vulnerabilities
screens.subtitle: Avoid non-deterministic operations and resource-heavy queries

narration.text: Chaincode must execute deterministically: given the same inputs, peers must produce the same read/write set. Non-deterministic operations such as using the current timestamp or generating random numbers on-chain can lead to inconsistent endorsements and ledger forks. If randomness is required, produce it off-chain and submit it as part of the transaction payload. Performance-wise, be cautious with wide scans like GetQueryResult over thousands of records without indexes; these can time out or exhaust peer resources. Avoid loops over large datasets inside a single transaction; instead paginate or perform batched operations across multiple transactions. Security vulnerabilities include missing access checks, insufficient input validation, and exposing existence of sensitive records unintentionally. To mitigate these issues: fail early, centralize checks, index queries, and prefer off-chain storage for large objects. Implement proper error handling and logging to help debug production issues without leaking sensitive data. As a closing question, ask whether your chaincode could be attacked by unauthenticated calls or cause a denial of service by expensive queries. If the answer is yes, identify the change needed to close that gap. Determinism, Performance, and Common Vulnerabilities means ensure deterministic execution, avoid heavy in-transaction scans, and close gaps in validation and authorization to prevent forks and performance attacks.. In practical terms, avoid non-deterministic operations and resource-heavy queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security rule
keyIdea.text: Ensure deterministic execution, avoid heavy in-transaction scans, and close gaps in validation and authorization to prevent forks and performance attacks.

content.html:
Deterministic execution

Avoid on-chain randomness and implicit timestamps. If you need external data, submit it as transaction input so all endorsers see the same values.

Performance cautions
  • Large GetQueryResult operations need indexes and pagination.
  • Avoid looping over many records in a single transaction.
  • Store large objects off-chain and keep hashes on the ledger.
Common vulnerabilities
  • Missing authorization checks on administrative functions.
  • Insufficient validation leading to invalid or inconsistent state.
  • Expensive queries enabling resource exhaustion.
Closing question
Can your chaincode be invoked by unauthorized callers or trigger expensive queries? If so, plan fixes now.

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you should remember. First, input validation ensures that all external values meet expected type, format, and range rules, preventing invalid state and runtime errors. Second, access control requires explicit checks of the transaction submitter using MSP ID and attributes, typically through the Client Identity utilities, to stop unauthorized operations. Third, state management is about designing keys, composite keys, and lean JSON so queries and updates are efficient; large binaries belong off-chain. These three ideas — validate, authorize, and model for queries — are the bedrock of secure and performant chaincode. Keep these concepts in mind as you write and review smart contracts, and pair them with unit and integration tests plus a clear upgrade strategy to maintain safety over time. Key Concepts means validate inputs, enforce identity-based permissions, design lean state, test comprehensively, and plan safe upgrades.. In practical terms, essential takeaways from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs, enforce identity-based permissions, design lean state, test comprehensively, and plan safe upgrades.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.2 › Key Concepts
Input Validation
Check presence, type, format, and range for every external parameter.
Access Control (CID)
Use MSP IDs and attributes via the Client Identity APIs to enforce permissions.
State Management
Design composite keys, indexes, and keep ledger data lean; reference large objects off-chain.
Takeaway

Combine validation, explicit authorization, efficient state design, testing, and upgrade planning to produce reliable chaincode.

narration.text: These final concepts reinforce testing, deterministic execution, and performance awareness. Unit tests using the mock stub let you validate logic and authorization quickly. Integration tests on a temporary network validate endorsement policies, peer behavior, and upgrade paths. Deterministic execution is essential: avoid in-chain randomness and implicit timestamps; submit any external values as transaction inputs so all endorsers see the same data. Performance considerations include avoiding large in-transaction scans, indexing CouchDB queries, and keeping on-ledger data minimal. Together these practices guard against ledger forks, slow peers, and vulnerabilities. As you finish this chapter, plan a checklist: add validation helpers, centralize authorization, design composite keys, write unit and integration tests, and create migration helpers for upgrades. That checklist will be a practical guide the next time you write or review chaincode. Key Concepts — Continued means test thoroughly, keep execution deterministic, index queries, and monitor for performance hotspots to ensure stable chaincode in production.. In practical terms, testing, determinism, and performance. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Final summary
keyIdea.text: Test thoroughly, keep execution deterministic, index queries, and monitor for performance hotspots to ensure stable chaincode in production.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.2 › Key Concepts — Continued
Unit & Integration Testing
Mock the stub for unit tests and validate deployment logic with integration tests on a temporary network.
Determinism
Ensure identical execution across endorsers by avoiding on-chain randomness and implicit timestamps.
Performance Awareness
Index queries, paginate results, and avoid expensive loops over large datasets to protect peer resources.
Action checklist

Add validation helpers, centralize authorization, model keys for queries, write tests, and include migration steps for upgrades.

ai_generation_note:
Produce a 10-minute live coding video demonstrating chaincode development best practices in Go. Start with a basic `TransferAsset` function and progressively add: 1) Client Identity (CID) based access control (only `Org1MSP` can invoke), 2) Robust input validation for `newOwner` and `assetID` (non-empty, asset exists). Show how to retrieve the client's MSP ID using `ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID()`. Include terminal commands to package and install the chaincode, and then invoke it from `peer` CLI, first successfully, then with invalid inputs/unauthorized user to demonstrate errors. Use a split-screen view for code and terminal. Conclude with a reflection prompt on the importance of security-first chaincode design.
